raw_case_text:
A 50-year-old uneducated male of low socioeconomic status was scheduled for amputation of toes. To start with, he had complaint of fever associated with chills and rigors for 3 weeks. He consulted a local practitioner who prescribed some tablets about which patient could not give the details. He noticed blackening of toes of both the feet, which was slow and progressive over 1 week. As he was not responding to the treatment, he was rushed to our medical college. There was no history of trauma, significant drug ingestion particularly ergot, alcohol consumption or smoking. On physical examination, he was febrile, dehydrated, and had pallor; there was no icterus, cyanosis, edema, or significant lymphadenopathy. A pulse rate of 120/min, respiratory rate of 24/min, and blood pressure of 90/70 mmHg was recorded. All peripheral pulses were palpable. On systemic examination, mild hepatosplenomegaly was present and rest of the systemic examination was normal. On local examination, there was blackish discoloration of all toes, extending up to malleoli [Figures 1 and 2]. Intavenous line was secured. Ringer lactate was started and investigations were sent for. Reports were as follows [Table 1].
Peripheral blood smear showed ring forms of P. falciparum with occasional gametocytes. Three consecutive blood cultures for bacteria were negative. Color Doppler study of the lower limbs revealed normal flow in both the femorals and the popliteal, with slightly reduced flow in tibial and dorsalis pedis artery with hypoechogenic shadow in its lumen.
The patient was given i.v. quinine, loading dose of 20 mg/kg followed by a maintenance dose of 10 mg/kg thrice a day for 2 days. Then, the patient was shifted to oral quinine (dose 10 mg/kg) thrice a day and oral paracetamol 500 mg thrice a day for 5 days. Two units of packed cell transfusion were also given. Fever subsided within 5 days of treatment. His peripheral smear for malarial parasite became negative after 7 days of quinine course. Line of demarcation did not progress any further. For management of gangrene, amputation was planned. All repeated blood investigations were within normal limits except prothrombin time 16.5 s, fibrinogen level 2.9 g/L (normal value 1.5-4 g/L), and D-dimer 1.7. The surgery was done under total i.v. anesthesia.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old male presenting with a 3-week history of fever with chills and progressive blackish discoloration of all toes of both feet for 1 week.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced fever with chills and rigors for 3 weeks and took unspecified oral tablets from a local practitioner without relief. Over the preceding week, he noticed slow, progressive blackening of all toes on both feet. Upon presentation, he was dehydrated and hypotensive with bilateral symmetrical peripheral digital gangrene.
subjective.past_medical_history: Low socioeconomic background. Denied history of trauma, ingestion of ergot alkaloids or other vasospastic drugs, tobacco smoking, or alcohol consumption.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, rigors, and bilateral toe pain and blackish discoloration. Negative for chronic peripheral vascular symptoms or Raynaud's phenomenon. Medications: unspecified tablets from local practitioner. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile, dehydrated, marked pallor; no icterus, cyanosis, edema, or significant lymphadenopathy. Pulse rate: 120 beats/min, respiratory rate: 24 breaths/min, blood pressure: 90/70 mmHg. All peripheral pulses were palpable. Abdomen: Mild hepatosplenomegaly. Local examination: Symmetrical blackish discoloration (dry gangrene) of all toes extending up to the malleoli bilaterally.
objective.routine_investigations: Three consecutive bacterial blood cultures: Negative. Repeat laboratory panel post-stabilization: Prothrombin time (PT): 16.5 seconds, serum fibrinogen: 2.9 g/L (reference: 1.5-4 g/L), D-dimer: 1.7.
objective.advanced_workup: Color Doppler ultrasonography of lower limbs: Normal flow in bilateral femoral and popliteal arteries; slightly reduced flow in tibial and dorsalis pedis arteries with hypoechoic luminal thrombus/shadow.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by symmetrical peripheral digital gangrene of bilateral feet and microvascular thrombosis.
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood smear demonstrated ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum with occasional gametocytes (smear cleared and became negative after 7 days of quinine). Bacterial blood cultures were negative; ergotism, Raynaud's disease, and macrovascular thromboembolism were excluded clinically and by duplex ultrasonography.
Plan & Outcome: Initial hemodynamic resuscitation with intravenous Ringer's lactate and transfusion of 2 units of packed red blood cells. Treated with intravenous quinine (loading dose of 20 mg/kg followed by maintenance dose of 10 mg/kg three times daily for 2 days), transitioned to oral quinine (10 mg/kg three times daily) with paracetamol (500 mg three times daily) for 5 days. Defervescence occurred within 5 days and parasite clearance at 7 days. Once the gangrenous line of demarcation stabilized, bilateral toe amputations were successfully performed under total intravenous anesthesia.
